description: We are DW Space, team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are working on the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge, focusing on combining interactive web technology, data visualization, and decision-support logic using NASA Earth observation data.
summary: TaniNusa 3D is an interactive 3D web decision-support simulator built for smallholder farmers in East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), Indonesia, one of the country’s most drought-prone agricultural regions. By integrating NASA POWER agroclimatology, SRTM elevation data, and live NASA GIBS satellite imagery into a two-layer FAO-56 Penman-Monteith water-balance and Growing Degree Days (GDD) pest-risk model, the platform simulates root-zone soil moisture and climate stress across local terrain. Instead of relying on guesswork under erratic rainfall, farmers and agricultural extension workers can test and select resilient crop rotations tailored to specific microclimates, reducing crop failure risks and improving seasonal water efficiency.
details: Smallholder farmers across semi-arid East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), Indonesia face a short, erratic monsoon window (Dec–Mar) followed by up to seven dry months, leading to repeated monoculture maize failures, topsoil desiccation, and slope erosion. TaniNusa 3D bridges NASA Earth observations and local agronomy across four distinct agroecological zones (Kupang & TTS, East Sumba, Manggarai, Malaka & Belu) plus custom farm coordinates. Powered by NASA POWER agroclimatology and live API queries (PRECTOTCORR, T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, RH2M, WS2M, GWETROOT, GWETTOP) and SRTM elevation, the engine computes monthly FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0, a two-layer soil water balance (0–5 cm topsoil germination vs. 0–100 cm root-zone storage), FAO-33 drought yield response, Modified Fournier rainfall erosivity, and Growing Degree Days (GDD) for fall armyworm risk. Users inspect live NASA GIBS WMTS tile mosaics (VIIRS True Color, MODIS 8-Day NDVI, MODIS LST), test historical NTT El Niño sequences (2015–2017) with year-over-year Soil Organic Matter (SOM) carryover, and review explicit satellite data gaps and field-validation checks.
